strengths: Novel conceptual contribution reframing model merging from 'non-interference' to 'synergy', with strong empirical support (r=0.863 correlation in Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across vision (8/14/20 tasks), dense prediction, and NLP with consistent SOTA results, especially at scale (88.6% on 20 tasks)
Well-motivated rejection of entropy minimization (Figure 4) with clear demonstration of instability, effectively justifying the expert-guided self-labeling approach
Strong transferability analysis (Table 4) showing adapted layers provide substantial gains when applied to other merging methods (+10.5%p, +7.6%p)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating complementarity between merging coefficients and task-specific layer optimization (Table 5, Figure 5)
Robust evaluation including corrupted data experiments and analysis across multiple model scales (ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, ResNet-50, RoBERTa-base)
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: the method is relatively straightforward (joint optimization of one layer + coefficients with expert-guided self-labeling), representing an incremental improvement over AdaMerging

Confounded contributions obscure true impact: sequential update strategy alone improves baseline by 1.5%p (80.1→81.6%), and confidence-based filtering contribution is unclear; hard to isolate core contribution

Expert-guided self-labeling has fundamental limitations: performance constrained by expert model quality, no principled expert selection, and Figure 6a shows mixed experts (0.8 coefficient) outperform pure experts

Weak theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 relies on unvalidated CTL assumption and provides only intuitive insights via straightforward Jensen's inequality application; improvement bound may be negligible in practice

Insufficient justification for design choices: why single-layer adaptation is optimal lacks theoretical grounding, cross-task performance metric choice not fully justified, multiple-layer training failure unexplained

High hyperparameter sensitivity with task-specific settings (learning rates: 0.01/0.001 for vision, 0.0005 for NLP; initial coefficients: 0.3 for 8 tasks, 0.1 for 14-20 tasks), reducing claimed simplicity and limiting guidance for new domains
Limited failure case analysis: only SVHN/MNIST overlap mentioned; smaller improvements on NLP tasks (83.9% vs. 81.6% for ProbSurgery) not adequately discussed

Incomplete evaluation: only 3 dense prediction tasks (all from NYUv2), dense evaluation limited in breadth; some reported improvements are marginal with small reported standard deviations (±0.1) without significance testing

Missing ablations: contribution of confidence-based filtering not quantified across domains, CTL assumption not empirically validated, sequential vs. simultaneous update impacts on non-vision tasks not evaluated

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8/14/20 vision tasks, dense prediction, and 8 NLP tasks with detailed per-task analysis
Clear empirical motivation from pilot study showing strong correlation (r=0.863) between cross-task performance and merge quality
Consistent improvements across domains with particularly strong results on dense prediction tasks where prior methods struggled
Thorough ablation studies including layer selection analysis, loss function comparisons, convergence analysis, and sparsity visualization
Excellent transferability analysis demonstrating adapted layers from SyMerge boost other merging methods (e.g., +10.5% on TA encoder)
Effective demonstration that self-labeling maintains gradient signal stability better than entropy minimization (Figure 4)
Solid experimental methodology with detailed hyperparameters, reproducibility statement, and extensive appendices
weaknesses: Incremental novelty over AdaMerging (Yang et al., 2024b): core difference is jointly optimizing layer+coefficients and using self-labeling instead of entropy—both are straightforward extensions
Weak theoretical justification: Proposition 1 assumes unvalidated cross-task linearity, applies only Jensen's inequality (not deep), and doesn't explain why single-layer adaptation works
Modest empirical improvements: 0.7% on 8 vision tasks (90.1% vs 89.4%), 2.3% on NLP (83.9% vs 81.6%) without statistical significance testing despite reported standard deviations

Critical implementation details buried in appendix: sequential updates alone yield ~1.5% gain (80.1%→81.6% for AdaMerging), confidence filtering adds complexity, making component contribution unclear and baseline comparison questionable

Misaligned framing: 'synergy vs. non-interference' distinction is philosophical; paper doesn't mechanistically demonstrate synergy, only that performance improves; Figure 6a shows merged models slightly outperform individual experts, undermining the 'expert-guided' narrative

Disconnect between pilot study (supervised, training data) and actual method (unsupervised, test data): pilot doesn't directly validate final approach; connection between insights and implementation is unclear
Incomplete ablations in Table 5: doesn't isolate contribution of sequential updates, confidence filtering, self-labeling, and layer adaptation separately; unclear which components drive improvements
Significant practical limitation not adequately discussed: method requires unlabeled test data access, unavailable in many real-world scenarios; no computational overhead analysis
Hyperparameter sensitivity: coefficient initialization changes from 0.3→0.1 for 14/20 tasks, domain-specific learning rates, suggests brittleness not well-characterized
Limited failure analysis: some tasks show significant degradation (Figure 7); minimal discussion of when/why method fails or performance degrades

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation with strong empirical correlation (r=0.863) between cross-task performance and merge quality; excellent pilot study design
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (vision 8-20 tasks, dense prediction, NLP) and architectures (ViT, ResNet, RoBERTa) demonstrating consistent SOTA performance
Thorough empirical justification of technical choices, particularly convincing comparison of self-labeling vs entropy minimization (Figure 4) showing entropy's instability during training
Exceptional transferability analysis (Table 4): adapted layers transfer effectively to other merging methods (+10.5% TA, +7.6% AdaMerging), demonstrating genuine functional alignment improvement
Well-designed ablation studies (Tables 5, Figure 5) clearly showing complementarity of joint optimization and why single-layer outperforms multi-layer training
Conceptually valuable reframing from non-interference to synergy, moving beyond defensive goals to seeking positive task interactions
Scalable to many tasks with robust performance degradation compared to baselines; practical test-time only approach without additional modules
Honest discussion of limitations acknowledging dependency on expert quality; thorough appendix with implementation details and code release commitment
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Proposition 1 relies on strong cross-task linearity assumption and proof is straightforward Jensen's inequality application; gap between theory (synergy helps) and algorithm (optimizes self-labeling loss)

Strong practical dependency on expert model quality; Figure 6a shows optimal performance at coefficient 0.8 (merged) not 1.0 (individual), creating potential circularity; no principled solution for weak experts

Under-explored design choices: confidence-based filtering important but details relegated to appendix without clear justification; sequential vs simultaneous updates attributed to catastrophic forgetting without rigorous validation

Entropy minimization comparison lacks mechanistic explanation of failure modes—insufficient analysis of whether degradation stems from overfitting proxy, distribution shift, gradient misdirection, or combination

Limited failure mode analysis: SVHN shows limited gains in Figure 3b (attributed to MNIST overlap) but insufficient investigation of when synergy fails; no systematic analysis of conflicting task pairs
Computational costs not documented: no timing comparisons with baselines, no memory requirements during test-time optimization, deployment costs unstated
Dense prediction experiments somewhat limited to single dataset (NYUv2) with only 3 tasks; stronger validation with diverse dense prediction benchmarks would strengthen generalization claims

Presentation issues: complex notation (θ, τ, λ) could be clearer; connection between pilot study protocol and actual algorithm under-explained; some critical details (confidence filtering, loss comparisons) relegated to appendix

strengths: Clear conceptual contribution reframing model merging from non-interference to synergy, well-motivated by strong correlation between cross-task performance and merge quality (r=0.863)
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (vision with 8/14/20 tasks, dense prediction, NLP) showing consistent improvements and strong scaling properties
Well-designed pilot study (Figures 1-3) with clear progression from motivation to method, effectively demonstrating vulnerability of training-free methods and benefits of single-layer adaptation
Technical improvement over baselines: expert-guided self-labeling maintains stable correlation with ground truth throughout training, unlike entropy minimization which degrades (Figure 4)
Impressive handling of edge cases, particularly merging models from disjoint initializations (Table 5) where existing methods fail
Extensive ablations and analyses with proper statistical reporting (mean ± std over 5 runs), thorough robustness studies to corrupted/backdoored experts and data scarcity
Practical efficiency: adds only 0.39M parameters, maintains computational efficiency comparable to lightweight baselines
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Proposition 3.1 entirely relies on cross-task linearity assumption from prior work; proof is straightforward and does not explain why single-layer adaptation specifically works
Critical mechanistic gap: no principled explanation for why single-layer adaptation is superior to alternatives; Figure 6 shows multi-layer training degrades performance but lacks mechanistic insight

Dependency on external signals: requires unlabeled test data at inference and relies on expert model quality for self-labels; Table 7-8 show significant degradation with corrupted experts, limiting practical applicability

Experimental design concerns: sequential update strategy improves baseline AdaMerging by 1.6%p (Appendix B.1), raising fairness questions; different coefficient initializations for different task counts suggest possible unequal hyperparameter tuning effort

Insufficient analysis of cross-task linearity assumption: while Table G empirically validates it, paper lacks discussion of failure modes or applicability boundaries; unclear when assumption breaks down
Missing key ablations: no analysis of which task combinations benefit most from merging, limited failure case discussion, sparsity analysis (E.7) is interesting but peripheral to core contributions

Presentation and reproducibility: code availability promised but not provided at review; multiple hyperparameters and design choices (confidence filtering with relative thresholds) may be difficult to reproduce across different settings

strengths: Conceptually clear reframing from non-interference to synergy, well-motivated by empirical correlation (Figure 2: r=0.863)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across vision (8/14/20 tasks), dense prediction, and NLP with consistent improvements
Convincing analysis of entropy minimization's instability (Figure 4) justifying expert-guided self-labeling approach
Thorough ablations demonstrating both components are necessary and analyzing layer selection, expert robustness, data efficiency
Interesting findings on merging across different initializations (Table 5) and transferable cross-task adaptation (Table 4)
Practical efficiency: minimal parameters (0.39M), runtime comparable to lightweight baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines known techniques (coefficient optimization, single-layer adaptation, self-labeling) without substantial innovation

Weak theoretical contribution: Proposition 3.1 straightforwardly applies Jensen's inequality under restrictive CTL assumptions without practical guidance; bound improvement ε_ij/2 lacks characterization
Comparison fairness issues: sequential update strategy improves AdaMerging from 80.1%→81.6% but baselines compared at 80.1%; unclear whether gains from method or training strategy
Gap between pilot study (supervised, frozen encoder) and actual method (unsupervised pseudo-labels) inadequately justified
Insufficient exploration of expert quality dependency: artificial failure tests (Tables 7-8) don't address correlated expert failures; confidence filtering provides only 0.1-0.4%p improvement
Missing mechanistic understanding: no analysis of what single layer learns, when/why method fails, or evidence that claimed synergy (cross-task mappings) actually occurs
Ad-hoc design choices: different coefficient initializations (0.3 vs 0.1) lack justification; different initializations experiment (Table 5) uses only one task pair
Presentation issues: multiple motivations in Section 2.2 without clear integration; implementation details scattered across main paper and appendices
Statistical concerns: some improvements within reported standard deviations (±0.1-0.4%); no significance testing against baselines
Reproducibility: code not provided; sequential update strategy and confidence-based filtering underspecified in main text

strengths: Compelling conceptual shift from non-interference to synergy with strong empirical motivation (Figure 2: r=0.863 correlation between cross-task and merge performance)
State-of-the-art results across diverse domains: vision (90.1% on 8 tasks), dense prediction, and NLP, with robust scaling to 20 tasks
Well-justified design choices demonstrated through clear analysis: entropy minimization correlation degrades post-training while self-labeling maintains alignment (Figure 4)
Remarkable capability to merge models from different initializations where standard methods fail (Table 5: 79.1% vs 5.4% AdaMerging)
Lightweight and efficient: only 0.39M trainable parameters yet outperforms WEMoE (7.16M), with memory comparable to AdaMerging
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive ablations, robustness tests (corrupted/backdoored experts, limited data, distribution shifts), and analyses across multiple dimensions
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, intuitive figures, and honest limitation discussion
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: self-labeling is standard (Lee et al., 2013), merging coefficients follow AdaMerging closely, single-layer adaptation is straightforward; main contribution is conceptual reframing rather than technical innovation

Theoretical contributions are incremental: Proposition 3.1 under cross-task linearity assumption shows that synergy tightens Jensen bound, but CTL only verified empirically in limited CLIP ecosystem, not proven generally

Significant dependence on expert quality: corrupted expert causes 12.8%p performance drop (90.1% → 77.3%, Table 7); backdoored experts show 75.6% off-task ASR, highest among adaptive methods (Table 8)
Test-time adaptation requirement limits applicability: needs unlabeled test data, restricting use in privacy/latency-sensitive settings; performance without TTA unclear

Incomplete design analysis: no deep explanation for why single layer suffices (Figure 6 empirical only); limited exploration of layer selection; hyperparameter choices vary per task setting (0.3 vs 0.1 initial coefficients), suggesting potential tuning requirements
Limited scope of 'different initialization' experiments: only one case (EuroSAT+DTD); does not validate across different architectures, training procedures, or domains
Sequential update strategy provides benefits (81.6% vs 80.1%) but is orthogonal to main contribution; attribution of gains is unclear
Confidence-based filtering mechanism (Appendix B.1) lacks theoretical justification; criterion is somewhat ad-hoc despite +0.4%p ablation gain
